title: Rohatsu 2013
speaker: Eko Jeff Kelley
summary: Our sense of identity and ego can create suffering by making us feel like we need to constantly assert ourselves and compare with others. In Zazen practice, letting go of this assertion allows us to see beyond our limited selves and connect with a more fluid and multifaceted true nature. By embracing this freedom, we can become more fully present and alive, without being held back by our attachments to specific roles or personas. This means we don't have to be bound by our usual identity or role, but can instead embody different aspects of ourselves as the circumstances call for it.

sentences.text: Good morning everyone.
It's nice to be here with you all.

I'll save the thank-yous for later and just want to say how much I've enjoyed these last couple days practicing here, with this wonderful opportunity to cultivate awareness, to open to what is, to dedicate ourselves to being present in each moment.
Yesterday Tim told us a story about the young woman Chiyono and her visit with the nun.
Part of the advice that the nun gave Chiyono was this.
*People are complete as they are.
If you don't fall into delusive thoughts, there is no Buddha and no sentient being.
There is only one complete nature.
If you want to know your true nature, you need to turn toward the source of your delusive thoughts.
This is called zazen.*
So we would all like to know our true nature, right?
That sounds pretty good.
We would all like to have the bottom of the bucket drop out.
But how do we do this?
How does this happen?
How do we cultivate this with our minds the way they are?
Is anyone tired of their mind yet?
They just keep going with the same thing and the same suffering, and our conditioning is so deep that it's hard to make headway.
It's hard to cut through.
It's hard to meet our lives in a different way.

And so I think sometimes we don't speak enough, or maybe I don't speak enough, about the nitty-gritty of working with our minds moment to moment, given the great momentum of our conditioning, the deep habitual nature of the way we think and the way we relate to our lives.
So we say things like, just open to what is, just allow the mind to settle and unfold.
These can be helpful.
I still think they are good suggestions.
But when our mind is just doing that same old thing again and again and our legs are hurting, those suggestions seem quite far away.
These suggestions do assume that we're making a very concerted effort to be present, a very dedicated effort to use our meditation focus to come back to the moment again and again.
Whether it's the breath or something else that we're working with, usually the breath.
So just really dedicating ourselves, especially in these two and a half days of sesshin, to return to that awareness, return to that focus again and again.
So we're cultivating awareness.
Our practice is a practice of awareness, and through this awareness our true nature unfolds.
We don't have to unfold it, but we need to be dedicated to cultivating this awareness again and again and again.
When we do this practice of returning to the breath, the mind will settle a bit.
Within that settled mind, our awareness is of a different sort than usual, and as things arise, we can see them more clearly.
We can see how they do cause suffering.
We can receive our thoughts or our old patterns as a knot of energy that comes into awareness.
As the mind is calmed down, we can allow that knot of energy to be conscious, fully conscious, and the knot dissolves and the energy is released.
These could be just micro insights that we see.
But until we've calmed the mind to some extent through this dedicated practice, it's hard for this insight to unfold.
The least little disturbance can be a knot of energy that we receive and touch with our awareness and have it open.
Now, some knots are bigger than others, right?
Some aspects of our habitual thinking are quite a constellation of energy.
I'd like to talk about one of those today, and that's our sense of being a person, personhood, I might call it.
It's like a sense of self, but this is a little more specific, perhaps.
It's like what we would call an identity.
But this is just our sense of being a particular person in the world.
I'm going to look at it today with you as something we're a bit too attached to, perhaps, and that we can afford to let go of.

Whenever we say something like, "Well, I may not be like that, but at least I'm like this," whenever we have any kind of evaluative or comparative thought, we are asserting ourselves as a certain kind of person in the world.
I think those thoughts are prone to come up anytime, and I think they're prone to come up during sesshin.
"I may not be a super practitioner, but I'm a pretty good practitioner.
I may not be a pretty good practitioner, but I'm not hopeless.
I may be hopeless, but please, I don't want to think that."
Regardless of the person that we believe ourselves to be, we're still asserting that.
We're putting that forward in the face of some experience, some onslaught of life events.
"I may not be like this, but I'm pretty sure I'm like this.
I may not be a hero, but I'm a pretty good person, pretty good father, pretty good grandmother."
But when I assert this, it's constantly getting challenged and eroded, and it needs constant reassurance, this assertion of personhood.
I have a picture of my son when he's six or so, and he's going like this.
It took me a while to see that what he had in the picture was this little Lego figure, this little action figure.
He's going like this.
That was common.
He was always advancing the action figure.
In the picture, it's just a tiny little thing, one of these little Lego men, and you can hardly see it, but it's as if he's kind of hiding behind it.
This is the action figure.
Here it is.
And meanwhile, of course, there's this multifaceted, dynamic human being.
But I think we all, in a way, are asserting this action figure.
Here's a Zen teacher action figure.
Here I am.
Look at me.
I'm ready for action.
But that's just this little figure, right?
This little tiny thing that I'm putting out there.
I'm this complicated, interconnected, so many different things, so many risings and passings away.
This little action figure of a Zen teacher, I think it's useful sometimes.
We hope it is, right?
But if I had to assert my Zen teacher action figure all the time, I would go nuts, I think.
I would be disloyal to so many parts of myself.
So we have our action figures.
Scientist action figures.
Pretty good mother action figures.
We are asserting these, and they may be more than just one thing, but there's still this certain person.
"I am like this.
I may not be this, but I'm at least like this."
And I'm asserting that person into the world.
Whenever we're evaluating ourselves in the sesshin, whenever we're comparing ourselves, it's this person that we're asserting.
I'm this person.
I think when children are young, they have to develop this, right?
I'm this person.
Maybe that's why they like to play with figures.
I can be this person.
In a way, we're hiding behind our little assertions of persons, our little action figures, and there's so much more going on.
I think we can feel that also this weekend.
So much more, when we let it seep in from the sides and the back and feel this one body, practitioners, this one body of life, this one life, this one nature that is animating and living us.
We can sense that as well.
But so often it's, "This is me, right?
This is me."
And so I'm suggesting that as the mind calms a little bit with our dedicated effort, we can see this assertion of being a specific person that we're kind of stuck on.
We feel the need to have this person that we continually assert.
The least mistake we make, the least inkling we have of something being wrong, that assertion meets with some resistance, and we put a lot of energy into putting that forward.
If you can feel that energy of asserting, we can ask ourselves, well, what is the energy that that assertion is meeting?
What is that opposing?
Is it some fear of life, some threatening of this world?
Why do we cling to this idea of a person that we continually assert to ourselves and to others?
And what if we were to stop?
Can we, in zazen, in our walking around [unclear: "Cixin"] life, can we let that go?
Can we just not assert anything for a moment?
Can we be nobody, and then in the next moment be somebody that we need to be?
But before we go into that more, let me bring forward a famous Zen story.
It's also in the Hidden Lamp book that Tim read from yesterday.
This one is a little more well known.
It involves Deshan, who was a great scholar of the Diamond Sutra.
He wasn't so much a Zen practitioner yet, but he was traveling south in search of the Dharma, carrying his commentaries on the Diamond Sutra with him.
So he had them in a bag, on his back or something.
In the course of his travels, he came across an old woman on the roadside selling tea and rice cakes.
He asked her, "Well, who are you?"
She said, "I'm an old woman selling rice cakes."
When he asked if he could buy some refreshments from her, she said, "Venerable priest, what are you carrying in your bag?"
He said, "Oh, I'm a scholar of the Diamond Sutra, and here I have all my notes and commentaries."
Hearing this, the old woman said, "I've heard that according to the Diamond Sutra, past mind is ungraspable, present mind is ungraspable, and future mind is ungraspable.
So where is the mind you wish to refresh with rice cakes, oh scholar?
If you can answer this, you may buy a rice cake from me.
If not, you'll have to go elsewhere for a refreshment."
Deshan was unable to reply.
He realized how stuck he was.
The old woman directed him to a Chan master nearby.
He went to practice Zen, and it says the next day he burned all his notes and commentaries.
So he really woke up here.
He realized, this scholar person that I am, it's just suffering.
It's not useless, but it's empty and so limited, and it hasn't connected me with what my heart most wants to connect with.
So he was right, and he had some intuition that, oh yeah, she's got it.
She's got me, and I'm burning these commentaries.
I'm putting away this action figure of the Diamond Sutra scholar and allowing myself to settle.
The tea lady here, and Joanna Macy has a nice commentary in the book, and she says:
*The tea lady is the Diamond Sutra itself, signless and limitless, aimless.
She is nobody we know and at the same time she is a manifestation of some wild and cranky freedom.
Through her there is no abiding and no attachment.*
So we don't know much about her past and future.
I have the sense that she is anybody that she needs to be.
She is wild and cranky and free, and if a little girl came up and asked to buy rice cakes, she would be a totally different person.
We don't know that much about her, but we know that she was able to hold a mirror to Deshan, and he was able to see his stuckness.
So in our practice, can we see this assertion, this figure that we're asserting?
Can we notice when we are carrying our accomplishments around in a bag?
Can we notice when we're carrying our ideas of ourselves, our good enough, pretty good, darn good, not very good ideas?
Can we see how limiting this is, how constraining, how much it needs asserting constantly and how much resistance there is to that assertion?

On a more subtle level, any time we're engaged in a conversation in our head, either rehearsing something or replaying something or imagining something, addressing someone or something, there's still this subtle assertion of being a particular person.
Maybe you're saying, "Well, I don't want to give up being who I am.
I don't want to give up being a person."
And that's good.
But I think what we're talking about here is, let's be the person that I am.
Let's be the person that you are, which is not constrained, not packaged up into a particular thing that needs constant assertion.
It's a living, fluid, open being that can manifest in many different ways at many different times.
So again, we might ask the question, "Fine, but I can see myself hanging on to an idea of a person.
Now what?
I'm aware of it, but I don't want to give it up.
Or I'm aware of it and it's not going away."
One thing we can do is investigate: what happens if I bring loving-kindness to this?

If I bring loving-kindness to this need I have to be a person of a certain type, a certain person, if I bring really unconditional loving-kindness to that, I think we'll find that that assertion becomes unnecessary, that insistence on being this person or that person becomes unnecessary.
We can be alive, we can be aware, we can meet the ingredients of the moment and not be so stuck, not hang on so tightly.
What happens if we say, "Boy, I really failed at that"?
We might take that the wrong way.

But what happens if we allow ourselves to be any person in any moment, a failure by some bizarre measure that we carry around, a person of the way, a loving parent, somebody who makes a silly mistake?
If we can let those go at each moment, how would that be?
So Deshan has another story at the end of his career, and teachers like to point to the career of Deshan, so this is nothing too original.

At the end of his career, when he's the old abbot of a center and he's in his declining years and other people are running the center, one day he's heading toward the eating hall with his bowls in hand, and one of the nice abbots, if you will, says, "Where are you going, teacher?
The bell hasn't rung yet."
He just simply turns around and goes back, and then there's a little conversation between two people about, well, what went on there?
They each have their ideas.
The next day he comes back and gives a talk like nobody has ever heard before.
But one of the points of the story is that he didn't need to be anybody.
He was a great Zen teacher, we can assume that, but at that moment, coming down the path with his bowls, he didn't need to be that.
He didn't need to be any particular person.
He didn't need to make some smart remark.
He didn't need to do anything except turn around and go back and wait for the time.
If we can see how we hold on to this personhood, continually push it forward, and then just let it drop, we can be this one life.
We can taste that freedom.
We can feel that relief in doing that for so long.
There's a phrase in Zen teaching that I like to use, and I find different ways to apply it.
I think it comes from something about Zhao Zhou, said that he uses the 24 hours rather than is used by them.
And so I think with our humanness, if you will, with our idea of personhood, can we use this skillfully in our bodhisattva work, in our loving-the-world work?
Can we use it and not be used by it, not be so needed so badly that we have to hang on to it and assert it in the face of so much resistance?
Can we be who the moment calls for?
Can we be simply the [unclear: "bower and chanter"]?
Can we be simply the person who eats, the person who serves, the person who is with their grandchildren, the person who is in front of a class, the person who is sitting reading a book?
We've been studying, well, we did a little brief unit on Avalokiteshvara in the class that we've been doing this fall.
One of her traits is that she manifests as anything, anything that's needed.
She has no form; she just comes as whatever is needed.
I'll read a little bit of this from the Lotus Sutra.
*If there are living beings in the land who need someone in the body of a Buddha in order to be liberated, Avalokiteshvara immediately manifests herself in a Buddha body and preaches the Dharma.
If they need a great general she becomes a great general.
If they need a petty king she becomes a petty king.
If they need a householder in order to be liberated she becomes a householder and preaches the Dharma.
If they need a monk and nun, a layman believer or a laywoman believer, immediately she becomes a monk and nun, a layman believer or a laywoman believer and preaches the Dharma.
If they need a rich woman, a householder woman, a woman chief minister, immediately she becomes these for them.
If the person needs a young boy or young girl to be saved, immediately she becomes a young boy or a young girl and preaches the Dharma.
If they need a heavenly being, a dragon, a human or a non-human, immediately she becomes one of those and offers the Dharma.*
So I think that was Avalokiteshvara as the tea lady, right?
She manifested as exactly the right person, and Deshan was very lucky to meet Avalokiteshvara as the tea lady, that wild and cranky expression of freedom.
But we can also be in our bodhisattva hood.
We can also manifest.
Our persons are not constrained by our ideas and our assertions.

To be a person in this world, to be a person of the way, is multi-faceted, multi-valent, multi-multi, and we can let go of that need to assert and then manifest in whatever person the situation requires.
I can manifest as a Zen teacher and do my best, but I can let that go, thank heavens, and just walk down the street as a person walking down the street.
So tonight is a big night, tomorrow is a big morning.
Just allow ourselves to manifest as the situation calls for.
Can we notice when we're carrying all this stuff around and set it down?
Can we be Deshan, who sees how stuck he is, and can we be the tea lady, who manifests as exactly the right being for the circumstances?
Can we let go and dance?
We're not holding on to this personhood that we're asserting.
It's an action figure, and we can be part of this fluid, unfolding, unifying, fruiting dance of the moment, and it's so wonderful that we can do this together.
